title: A cell is a battery. Why?
hook: Potassium leaks out of a cell, then stops. It was never blocked. What stopped it?

knows: diffusion moves particles from high to low concentration
doesNotKnow: that an ion gradient across a membrane builds a voltage that stops the net flow

misconception: Charged particles stop moving when concentrations are equal.
objective: The learner can explain that leaking potassium leaves the inside negative; the electrical pull back balances the concentration push at about -89 mV for 140 mM inside and 5 mM outside, and with equal concentrations the balance voltage is zero.
keyState: Leaked until balanced at 5 mM outside (-89 mV), then outside set to 140 mM where the balance voltage reads 0 mV.

claims.text: Toy model: only potassium ions (K+) can cross the membrane, at 37 C (body temperature). One dot is 5 mM; one + and - pair is 10 mV of voltage.
claims.source: Model choice in Demo.tsx; stated on the stage before the prediction ('Toy: only K+ leaks, at 37 C. 1 dot = 5 mM.'). Real cells also have sodium, chloride and pumps. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Demo.tsx: DOT = 5 mM, MARK = 10 mV, KT at 310.15 K; stage label 'Toy: only K+ leaks, at 37 C. 1 dot = 5 mM.'

claims.text: A cell holds about 140 mM potassium inside and about 5 mM outside.
claims.source: Typical mammalian cell concentrations (Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell; verify). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Alberts et al., MBoC, Table 11-1 (typical mammalian cell, K+ 140 mM inside, 5 mM outside; BioNumbers 106428 indexes this table). Other tables give 139/4; 'about' holds.

claims.text: With only potassium leaking, the balance voltage is E = (RT/F) ln(outside/inside); RT/F is 26.7 mV at 37 C, so 140 mM inside and 5 mM outside give about -89 mV.
claims.source: Nernst equation (Hille, Ion Channels of Excitable Membranes). node: RT/F = 26.727 mV at 310.15 K; 26.727 x ln(5/140) = -89.06 mV. Options -9 / -89 / -890 mV are E/10, E, E x 10 from the same function. The brief's -90 mV is the rounded value. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): node with CODATA R, F: RT/F = 26.727 mV at 310.15 K; 26.727 ln(5/140) = -89.06 mV; stage MV() shows -89 mV; options -9 / -89 / -890.

claims.text: Potassium leaving the cell leaves the inside negative; the negative inside pulls potassium back, and leaking stops when the pull equals the concentration push. Nothing moves net.
claims.source: Electrochemical equilibrium (Nernst); same sources as c3. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Electrochemical equilibrium at the Nernst potential: zero net flux (Hille, Ion Channels of Excitable Membranes, ch. 1).

claims.text: With 140 mM on both sides the balance voltage is 0 mV, because there is no concentration push to balance. On the stage, changing the outside level starts a fresh cell with no charge built up.
claims.source: ln(140/140) = 0, so E = 0 (node). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): ln(1) = 0 (node); reveal prints MV(nernst(140)) = 0 mV.

claims.text: Each leak press moves the voltage half of the remaining way to the balance voltage; real leaking takes milliseconds and moves a tiny fraction of the ions, so concentrations barely change and very few ions have to cross to build the charge.
claims.source: Toy dynamics in Demo.tsx (v + (E - v)/2). The statement about a tiny fraction of ions is a standard physiology fact (verify); the dot counts are not redrawn as the voltage builds. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Demo.tsx leak(): v + (e - v)/2. Derivation of 'tiny fraction': a 10 um cell, 1 uF/cm2, 90 mV moves Q = CV = 2.8e-13 C = 2.9e-18 mol, vs 7.3e-14 mol K+ inside (0.14 M x 5.2e-13 L): about 4e-5. Membrane time constant RC is milliseconds.

claims.text: The balance voltage follows the concentration ratio, about 61 mV for each factor of ten at 37 C; a 28 to 1 ratio (140 mM to 5 mM) gives about -89 mV.
claims.source: E = (RT/F) ln(out/in) with RT/F = 26.7 mV: 26.7 x ln 10 = 61.5 mV per tenfold; 61.5 x log10(5/140) = -89 mV.

recall.question: Potassium leaks out of a cell until it stops, with 140 mM inside and 5 mM outside. Why does it stop?
options: The charge it leaves behind pulls it back, balancing the concentration push
recall.why: Each potassium ion that leaves makes the inside more negative. At about -89 mV the pull back equals the push out, so net flow stops while the concentrations are still very different.
